reviewText: I've had this bag for two years or so, from the start when I first got my Canon EOS 60D camera. It's been with me ever since, going on trips to family gatherings and acting like a storage space for my gear when I'm at home. Over the years, I've expanded my personal photography collection by adding a 50mm prime lens in addition to the 18-135mm kit lens, a Canon 430EX II speedlite, extension tubes, remote triggers, cleaning kits, rechargeable batteries and their charger, lens caps and so on. All of the above plus more fits in snugly without issue. This bag is great for it's purpose - it holds a lot. Though I'm no pro, I carry around all of my equipment that can fit in the bag, plus accessories, software, booklets and more. The only things I cannot jam in it are large items like my softboxes, tripods and props. While I haven't treated the bag roughly enough to vouch for its superior sturdiness - it has not gone hiking or anything strenuous - mine is still in good condition. No zipper breakage, fraying, tearing. To wear, it's very comfortable, and a plus side to the design was the strapped front which allowed me to jam water bottles and snacks in the front for easy snacking while on the go. I do not use the straps underneath or on the sides for my tripod (a Sunpak 620-750TMBB Platinum Plus Tri-Monopod, Silver which is pretty hefty). It's unwieldy and the weight of the tripod causes it to sag on one side, and potentially slip free of the straps. Three of the issues I had with this backpack: 1.) I originally wanted a bag with a hammock system, such as the Case Logic SLRC-203 Large SLR Camera Bag (Black). The hammock really appealed to me as extra additional protection against sudden jarring. However, at the time I purchased this backpack, that sort of bag was not available. This backpack allows the camera to be placed at the top with the lens facing down, but it's not a hammock style and it is not, in my opinion, securely contained. Especially when I have my short 50mm prime lens on, the camera can shimmy loose and move around and potentially fall out. 2.) I also wanted a bag with a stable base. Be warned - this Canon backpack is NOT stable. Especially considering the bag can be top-heavy from the camera being placed on the top, it can and will fall over. This has always been my biggest concern, and I always take care to prop the bag up safely, or lay it down to prevent damage. More than anything, using a bag that causes me more need for concern than assuaging it, is a big loss in points for me. 3.) Should the bag fall forward, there is little to no padding on the front to cushion the fall. I've taken to putting booklets, DVDs and cleaning cloths in the pockets to help the padding, but it still makes me wince to see the bag tottering over. In short, after a few years of usage, I've finally put in the money and purchased a Kelly Moore Mimi Bag (Black). I wanted something to protect my gear while looking sophisticated enough to take out for social gatherings and family shoots, without branding the bag as a camera bag with lots of theft goodies in it to nab (that old Canon logo sure is obvious on this backpack!) That said, I will be keeping my Canon backpack at home to store items that I don't need for my every day use, and for those long trips where I need a bag that can carry some weight comfortably. And if it comes down to it, a bag that I won't mind scuffing up.
summary: Roomy and holds tons, but not quite my bag, baby

Bought this no-frills mobo to go in a work PC and read about them being reliable. Originally purchased from another retailer (that other PC parts retailer) and had to RMA - the RMA process takes horrendously long so ordered another w/ next-day shipping from Amazon. Amazon gets 5 stars as usual.

The problem with this motherboard is the 'cute' UEFI BIOS doesn't always... load. When I scrolled through items (RAM clocks, SATA mode, etc), some text fields were missing entirely, others were invisible (could still select, but couldn't see what you were selecting). All of this is a horrible sacrifice just to use a mouse in the BIOS - everyone's moving to this, and these companies' programming abilities aren't up to snuff to produce this functionality reliably. I figured I needed a BIOS update, done this several times, used the company's @BIOS software - failed, no diagnostic messages. Loaded BIOS to USB drive and loaded it in BIOS... bricked the motherboard. Horrible. Got a new one from the Zon and resolved not to touch anything, use standard BIOS settings, just because it's a work PC and I need to... work. Also, I had already installed a ton of software on my C drive and didn't want any hiccups. As a result, I have downclocked RAM, etc. Do not buy this unless budget is the only consideration.

That said, I've built ~8 PC's in the last 2 years and I couldn't name a reliable mobo manufacturer with a no-frills stability mentality. Maybe Intel? That's >$100 for same functionality as the overseas companies, and I've had a few fail on me as well.

***EDIT 12/29/14*** - THIS MOTHERBOARD HAS A KNOWN DEFECT involving the 'A2' diagnostic code that is shown pre-bios. Google 'MSI motherboard stuck on A2' to see what I'm talking about. About 3-6 months in, the motherboard fails to recognize attached SATA HDDs/SSDs and hangs before you're even allowed to see the BIOS. Resetting the CMOS, pulling various SATA devices, none of this works, and all the SSD/HDDs were connected to a spare PC I have in the back and they all worked flawlessly. The only solution I've found (this has happened to me TWICE now) is to replace the motherboard and plug all your devices into their previous slots - the PC then boots right up. Because this is a work system, uptime is critical and I will NEVER buy another MSI product (I currently own 4). I tried submitting a tech support ticket the first time it happened (in April) and they got back to me at the end of summer. Their support forums are full of MSI reps giving the standard 'did you test your power supply? did you run a memory diagnostic?' endlessly in circles while people eventually just buy new components. Spend an extra 60-100 and get whatever good ASUS/EVGA is out, their QC seems to be leaps and bounds above MSI's.

After doing lots of research, reading reviews of this and other telescopes, I decided on this one.
The people on the astronomy forums are snobs and hate anything that isn't a dobsonian.
I'm not necessarily saying being a snob is bad as I was a snob with cigars, but they would answer almost every question about should I buy this or that reflector or refractory scope with, neither buy a dobsonian. Their reasoningfor the most part made since. However, I did not want to spend the money for a dobsonian that can also track, not for my first telescope.

Unlike many people who reviewed this telescope, I watched the assembly and usage videos before purchasing. I also watched the assembly video while I assembled it, so for me, assembly didn't take long at all.

The usage video also showed me how to balance the scope on the mount, as well as aligning the scope with the view finder. Fortunately mine arrived in good shape, so I did not have to collimate it, but watched a video on how to do so.

The first time I took it out was last night 8/15/17. I spotted what I believed to be Saturn and unfortunately all I saw was a dot. I used the 25mm, 10mm, and Barlow lens, and nothing but a dot. I was very disappointed and wondered how long I had to return it.

The next morning, I checked the scope and view finder alignment, and set it again.
Tonight 8/16/17 I took it out again. When I spotted what I believed to be Saturn, I set up the scope, targeted the dot with the view finder, and looked through the 25mm lens. I saw a circle. Then I put in the 10mm lens, and there it was, Saturn.
I was so happy. Then I saw Jupiter, though I couldn't get a good view because of the trees.

At this point I am pleased with what I have seen and look forward to seeing more. I'll eventually get more powerful lenses.

Many reviews of this telescope complain of the vibration using the EQ2 mount. Unfortunately that is very true. While viewing Saturn and tracking it, it repeatedly lost focus due to the motion from turning the scope. It also gave the same visual vibration when turning the focus.
That is one of the many reasons the telescope snobs recommend dobsonian telescopes.

Overall, as my first telescope I am pleased. I know spending $300 and seeing visual vibration doesn't sound pleasing, but I am pleased with the view of Saturn and Jupiter, as well as being able to track them with this telescope.

The fitbit is pedometer, with a bluetooth connection. Its major functions are counting steps (which it can only show you in increments of 2000) and storing that information in a place where you can later view it by a better piece of technology. The fitbits battery life is advertised as up to 5 days. In my experience, its about 1-2 days. Thats right folks, this thing you need to charge every night (if you want reliability).  The indication of how much battery life is only visible when plugged in to the usb charger (at which point it can not count steps). Its up to 5 dots. It says that it should charge in 3 hours. My cell phone charges in less time then that, but when i put the fitbit after sleeping for 8 hours it is usually at 3 dots. So perhaps it changes in 16 hours (i don't know, i have other things to do in my life). When the fitbit runs out of battery sometimes it sends you and email, most of the time it does absolutely nothing except have the dots dance at you instead of show you the number of steps you have when you check. When you see the dancing dots, the fitbit is telling you that whatever steps you think you have gotten have been lost to space and time. Those steps have gone to a far away land never to been seen or heard of again. The fitbit usually syncs with your phone, but many times it doesnt. Instead your phone simply gives you a red icon and tells you that you need to be more active because you have 0 steps.
All in all this product is a disaster. It took at most $3 to manufacture, and boy you can tell... sadly i couldn't tell within the 14 day return policy at best buy.

Well Tom Tom doesn't really need to make the GPS units anymore because those have become obsolete in a way, so there is this item a golf watch.

1.  What's in the box?:  You receive the watch, also an instruction booklet, and a USB power charger.

2.  Aesthetic?:  The watch is sleek and nicely done for an electronic watch.  It has a nice square face, with a smooth band, a double clasp, and a button on the inside for the wrist. 3.  Set-up?:  The watch does not carry a charge, so you will need to charge it with the power cable.  After that, the watch comes on and away you go.  The watch goes through the initial set-up (use the arrow on the wristband) and this is pretty intuitive. 4.  Use?:  To use this on the golf course is easy.  I turned on the unit in terms of airplane mode being off and after a few beats, the watch finds the nearest gold courses and away you go.

reviewText:
Pro:  Low cost
Con: Not easy to work with
.  Deceptively thick wire but with a very small conductor
.  Unspecified conductor gauge

At first glance the unstripped wire looks like ~16 gage but the conductors are actually much smaller, 24 gauge at best. I used them for some short strips of LED lights and they work fine, but the unspecified small gauge wire certainly won't safely handle more than an amp or two.

The conductor are stranded copper and the assembly comes with very short (~1/16" - 1/8") prestripped/tinned leads.

The insulation is very thick and hard to cut /strip.  I have no idea what the actual insulating material is but it is definitely NOT normal PVC.

The wire is very difficult to strip. The insulation is much thicker than the conductor and the waxy plastic material does not cut cleanly. I also had to almost always cut off the pre-tinned portion of the wire since the cut piece of insulation won't slide off the wire end with the extra thickness of the solder on the lead.

I received this laptop today so this review is limited to just one topic:  The damn touchpad "tapping" function cannot be disabled via the Elan touchpad control options.  I purchased this laptop primarily for very fine video editing, which would be impossible with the ultra-sensitive touchpad "tap to select" function operational.

Fortunately I found a solution that someone named "rakulia" posted on-line.  The solution, however, requires editing of the PC's registry file--something that I hesitate to attempt but fortunately the change went well and, after a restart, worked perfectly.  Now I can have full control over the touchpad without accidentally initiating unwanted actions.

For those who need to disable the touchpad tapping function, go into "regedit" and make the following changes:
1.  Select registry file to edit: HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Elantech\SmartPad
2.  Then change Tap_Enable to 0 and Tap_Activate_Enable to 0
3.  Then reboot

If this PC provides the blazing video editing capability that I need, I may add ore info to this review in the future.

Update:  As of Sept 10, 2016, this laptop has been working very well and I've increased my rating to 4 stars.  Still not 5 due to the touchpad issue.  My primary requirement for this laptop is video editing.  I use Cyber Director for editing and the laptop speed is very good.  Previously the audio and video were out of sync when previewing editing changes, which made precise editing very difficult.  This laptop is able to provide previews that remain in sync.  Additionally, final production times have been cut almost in half.  A 15 minute video now takes only about 20 minutes to produce.

The look and feel of this laptop are also both excellent.  Amazon describes the case as satin gold, but you have to look vary hard to perhaps see the slight gold tinge so it has a very nice satin look.  The case, keyboard and overall feel of this laptop are all excellent.  It feels very sturdy and well designed.  It also seems to have excellent heat dissipation since the heat is directed out the sides, which reduces the potential for being blocked on the bottom.

Update:  Dec 10 2016,  After using this PC to do more than just video editing, I find the space bar can cause text editing errors.  After entering a paragraph of text, I've noticed that there are sometimes errors due to the lack of a space between words.  After doing a little testing, I've found that the far left and right areas of the space bar do not always work properly.  I can fully depress the lower left and lower right areas of the space bar and (sometimes) no space is produced.  Pressing the center of the space bar will always produce a space, but the lower left and right areas do not.  Perhaps this is an issue with just my keyboard, and it is only a minor annoyance, but for someone who does a lot of keyboard work it may be a more significant problem.  Otherwise, I remain very happy with this laptop and plan to start using it as my primary laptop.

So I got the Vizeri (which actually says "Tank007" inside the tube) based upon the excitement here. I'm not excited.

First of all, it's not even tactical! A tactical light works with a soft-press of the switch from the off position. This needs to be completely switched on to work...and then...changing modes by half-pressing the switch doesn't always work. It usually needs to be half-pressed TWICE in every mode, before it changes the mode.

With all due respect to those who are impressed by the Vizeri's brightness...you ain't seen nothin' yet! By comparison to the majority of flashlights on the market, 230 lumens isn't terribly bright. Many are over 500 lumens. In fact, I have a flashlight from Zebralight that is 3" tall, less than half the diameter of the Vizeri, operates on 1 AA battery, and is just as bright (if not brighter) than the Vizeri!

The Vizeri also displays PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) when operating in medium and low mode. The effect of PWM is seen when a fast moving object is being lit by the light. The object appears as a blurry, multiple image. If you ONLY operate this light on high...you'll never see it. The CREE XR-E Q5 LED was a technical breakthrough almost 10 years ago. It's not a bad LED, but it doesn't have the capacity to offer much more lumens than is already coming out of this light. It cannot drive a light as hard as the newer XM-L LED's. On the plus side, it has good throw. And the manufacturers have seen fit to not drive it hard enough to cause excess heat and premature burnout.

What I admire most about this package, is the accessories. They're quite generous. Especially the diffuser.

If you've never owned an LED flashlight before, or only had a really cheap one, then the VZ230 will seem pretty impressive. For someone like me, who owns many lights, it's pretty average and doesn't hold a candle in terms of convenient size or lumen output that most of my others do.

It's not a bad light, but it has some issues. The zoom works well and can be set at any interval you choose. The beam of the LED when zoomed out, is only useful when pointing at something 100ft or farther. This is due to the 'squared shape' of the LED which is seen in that mode.

You can use NiMH rechargeable batteries instead of disposable AAA's. You can also use lithium rechargeables; 2 16340's or 2 18350's. Disposable CR123's can also be used. Interestingly though, in my visual tests, I can't see any noticeable difference in lumen output with the lithium vs. the NiMH AAA's. In other words, it doesn't appear any brighter with lithium batteries. That surprised me.

I don't generally like or recommend "zoom" flashlights. Name-brand non-zooming lights can be bought for about the same price as this one. The beams on those lights are far more useful to me...and much brighter too!
summary: It's not ALL bad...even though it has PWM!

So I had wanted a way to hook up my Playstation 2 to my HDMI-only computer monitor. I tried a few converters, with varying results. This one works pretty well, though.

However, there is one caveat, but I'll get to that.

I plugged my PS2 via component cables into the box, and the audio cables into the box, and then the HDMI cable into my monitor (Asus VH236H in case you're wondering).

I got picture and sound perfectly via the single HDMI cable, which is great. Zero perceptible input lag is also great! I could play Hot Shots and Shadow Hearts (which require split-second timing) perfectly. Yay!

But now the downside...

Because the converter is also an upscaler, it upscales all 480i/480p PS2 signals to 720p. That in of itself is not a bad thing, as it really does look good. The downside is that everything is output in 16:9 widescreen. Yes, even games that are NOT widescreen. For games that are widescreen, this isn't an issue. But... well..., I personally don't like stretched games. On my Asus monitor, I cannot set the screen to display it in 4:3 non-widescreen with this converter box connected because it's a set digital signal. Boo.

Anyway, if you can live with it stretching non-widescreen images, you'll be fine.

4 stars out of 5.

The quality of sound coming thru my computer speakers is critical to me. The sound that comes from the "built in" sound devices on most mother boards today may provide the latest in 7.1 technology, but if you listen to music critcally as I do, there's just too much inherent noise. The answer is an add-on sound card. I prefer the ease of connection from the front bay interface that the Creative card provides. All the connections for audio are there, digital and analog, except the XLR type. If you need those, other external devices can provide that. Now, I'm not a gamer, so you may ask "why did you purchase a 'gamer' sound card?" Well, the quality afforded  this card is not lost on me. My studio is capable of producing 5.1 surround mixes of the music I record. To mix them down I need an exacting device with stellar specs. My choices were few in the price range I wanted. The front access drive bay was the deciding factor.
This sound card connected to my Logitech Z-5500 speakers brings my listening experience to new heights of clarity. The built-in "Crystalizer" adds impact and clarity and has a wide range of adjustment.
Of course it can be shut off too, but once you hear the difference, you'll probably choose to have at least some level of enhancement. This is the best sound card I've ever purchased, and as long as motherboards provide a PCI slot, any upgrades I make, I'll be swapping this sound card over. Amazon.com's price with the free shipping was my deciding factor where to purchase. My local stores wanted 199.99 for the card. Amazon beat that by 25.00.

I live in an older house and neighborhood with old overhead power lines and transformers. Voltage sags when people run their air conditioners and these units work well for boosting voltage.

I own six of the older model SS1200 which has the rectangular case. The newer ones have a trapezoidal-shaped case. I have not had any problems with the older models, but I would have to say that the capacity is rather low and it is worthwhile to consider the SS2000 if you're planning to plug in more than 5.5A total draw. The SS2000 uses the same case and has a heavier-gauge power cord, although it still seems to be the bare minimum for the rated 9.1A. However, I ordered 2 of the newer SS2000s and had problems with both (see my review of the SS2000 for details).

The last SS1200 that I bought had a cracked rear panel but is still safe to use as the crack is in the mounting hole. This is due to how these units are packaged and handled during shipment. The cord and plug are packaged at the back of the unit, and if it's dropped during shipment on the back panel, the weight of the transformer causes the plug to crack the panel. I suspect that the type of polymer used in the case has changed.

Also, if you get a lemon, Amazon cannot take these units back even though they are not a UPS and do not contain a lead-acid battery. Amazon sent a replacement, but after the second one was also a lemon, they referred me to the manufacterer which I would have to RMA and send back for repair at my cost.
summary: Newer models seem lacking in quality

These are very similar to other Bluetooth headphones as far as features go, however where they stand out is the incredibly snug and comfortable fit.  They are easy to re-seat if they work loose; the earphone tips are mounted to the "tube" with the clip on it and it's just a matter of grabbing that tube and using it as a handle to readjust the position or seal.  Of the wireless Bluetooth headphones I've tried these are definitely the most comfortable and I have been able to wear them all day without any irritation or pain.  As far as sound quality goes I am very happy with the evenly balanced bass/treble, there is enough bass without it being so strong as to overshadow the other frequencies.  --These headphones are not something that you would buy because they have tons of bass, they are in-ear headphones that form a seal with your ear to block out a lot of the noise around you, and part of that effect is that is to limit the amount of bass a bit.
Battery life seems to be around the 8-hour mark, as expected.  I did notice one odd effect when the battery was very low: the headphones would constantly disconnect/reconnect from the phone and since it uses a synthesized voice it would say "Connected to phone"/"Disconnected" over and over.  Not a big deal, just a little odd.

My only gripe about the sound is not related to its quality but because when you adjust the volume it sends commands to the phone/tablet you're connected to, adjusting the system volume instead of leaving that as-is and allowing you to go in several steps from complete silence to the current system volume.  The main drawback is that (For me anyway) it's not possible to adjust the volume below a what I consider a fairly loud level-- it's that or mute the audio completely.  Maybe for others that is as low a volume as they would want to listen to, but I have fairly sensitive ears and it's annoying not being able to adjust it to a lower volume than that.

Overall these are really excellent headphones and I look forward to using them in the noisy environments I sometimes work in.  Full disclosure: I received these headphones to evaluate after having some problems with the ones I originally purchased (A different model); Taotronics was very helpful and responsive in resolving the issue.
summary: Great quality headphones for a great price

I am a delivery driver and the radios installed in our vehicles are quite poor. I have issues pulling in all but the most powerful local stations with them. I love listening to NPR and unfortunately I was unable to receive my local affiliate. After getting tired of driving in silence for 8 hours a day I decided to have a look at portable units with excellent reception. This seems to be the best.

The built in antenna is not great, but usable if you like to listen to powerful commercial stations that are close by. Plugging in a pair of headphones improves things a bit as the unit uses the audio cable as an antenna. Things really get impressive when you use the dedicated external antenna that is included with the unit. It's a simple wire with a standard 1/8" jack. To give you an idea of the reception capability with the external antenna, I have had no trouble at all pulling in WELH, a 4,000 watt station from over 20 miles away. Typical commercial stations are normally 10 times more powerful. Your results will obviously vary due to terrain and other factors.

A smart choice by C-Crane here: there is a switch to select between the speaker, and stereo or mono sound through headphones. This means you can use a pair of headphones solely as an antenna and have the the audio sent through the built-in speaker. In other words, plugging in headphones does not automatically mute the built in speaker. You have to select that manually. The built in speaker is adequate for talk radio but I find it poor for music. It's also slightly too quiet for my liking. I'm basically nitpicking here, though. This is a POCKET radio!

Build quality seems good. The edge is rubberized but I'm not sure how effective that is. I have dropped it once and the batteries popped out but there has been no damage. The unit is quite light so if it's dropped from a short height I don't think much damage will be done. Unfortunately it's rather bulky. I didn't like the feel of it when using the belt clip. This is most likely a trade-off between performance and portability and I'm quite glad that C-Crane opted for the former. What's the point in a sleek radio if it doesn't pull in stations you like?

The button layout is intuitive. The lock switch is a great feature if you're going to be putting it in your pocket. It disables ALL button functions, including the power button. I would have preferred a switch for the power button, as it's rather easy to accidentally turn it off if you have it unlocked (which I prefer, so I can easily switch between preset stations).

Shuffling through the preset pages is rather odd. Only 5 presets are available at any one time. To enable more memory presets without having an overwhelming amount of buttons, C-Crane opted for digital memory "pages". To access these pages, you must press and hold the BAND button and then select a page using the preset buttons. In practice this is rather cumbersome, especially if you want to select a preset station without looking at the screen. I would have preferred some sort of system where you could cycle through the preset pages sequentially.

Now that I've been using the radio for a while I can comment on the battery life. With the speaker on full volume, playing 8+ hrs a day, the battery has lasted just up to two weeks. That's impressive. I'm down to one bar now and I could probably go a bit longer, but I think reception isn't as good with the weak batteries (but maybe I'm imagining things). With headphones I assume the batteries would last MUCH longer, as those tiny speakers aren't as difficult to drive.
summary: Probably one of the best pocket radios out there

The local computer superstore did not have an ordinary mechanical KVM switch available, so I went with the Belkin on the strength of their reputation.  Unfortunately, certain assumptions are made in the design of this unit that cause it to be poorly suited to use with my setup; I'm trying to control a docked Dell D600 laptop and a Compaq desktop from the same keyboard, mouse and monitor.  There are several issues involved which the instructions don't take into account.  First, the KVM switch wants to use the same keystroke as part of its selection sequence that the laptop wants to use as a control signal emulation; the "scroll lock" key.  This caused the need to select a different key for the laptop's control signal, which had its own set of issues as a result.  Second, it turns out that the KVM switch is picky about the timing of the two keystrokes needed to swap from one system to the other; lag too long between keystrokes, or try to swap back too soon, and the sequence gets ignored.

I wish I had saved the packaging and receipt; this purchase would be going back to the store if I had, but some of the problems didn't become apparent for a couple of weeks because one of the computers involved wasn't present right away.

I'm going to replace this gadget with a mechanical switchbox from a different source.

These have a lot of metal in them, yes. A lot of people seem to equate that with quality and durable construction, and that might be true in part. But they're extreeemely heavy. The controls on the outside of the right ear piece are also a problem due to the plastic. When you press any of the buttons (they're all under one plastic piece that presses wherever you push it, like an Apple mouse) with the headphones on your head, it's insanely loud as the clicking sound of the button travels right through the hollow plastic and into your ear.

Third issue: sound quality
I will say my expectations were probably too high for headphones at this price point. They do have a lot of bass which is nice, but the sound is like swimming in mud because of it. And the "3D sound" effect sounds terrible.

Even if my expectations were too high, this low cost is not worth it to me. I'd rather spend more money and be pleased with higher quality than spend all my time rationalizing something that sucks by saying, "Well, it was really cheap though."

This Jango speaker provides good sound quality, a variety of connection options, and decent portability. However for every good feature, it leaves something to be desired, falling short of greatness.

First of all the sound quality is good, and does not have any hickups, distortions, and so on. However it also sounds little bit flat. It seems like the speaker is designed more for bass - at least it sound like that for me. I think this is to provide more "loud" sound, however at least providing an equalizer would have been good.

The wireless connectivity has been designed with Jango ecosystem in mind. I had good success with both Android and iOS version of the Jango software, and the provided music selection, and radio streams are decent. However that's all about it, and the speaker would not directly become a main output (i.e.: AirPlay). I have some stations that are only on TuneIn, and I would prefer to have them streamed easily.

Fortunately this speaker also has bluetooth connectivity. However it means only one device at a time (so no iPad + my phone selectively), and in my experience there is a noticeable delay in bluetooth streaming.

The third option is the half-implemented DLNA connectivity. I was able to use Windows Media Player on my PC to play some of my content. However there was no option from my Mac at all. (I think there are some third party programs, but I currently do not have them). So this means no output from my MacBook except from bluetooth (remember: one device only on bluetooth).

And of course it's always possible to use a direct line in connection, yet this is obviously very limiting.

Overall, I would have preferred a proper DLNA + AirPlay connectivity. I don't believe the licensing cost would be too much, and given this device aims to be high end, their lack is very noticeable.

If you plan to stay in the Jango ecosystem, or the connection options would be sufficient in your case this is a very good device. For a versatile wireless speaker, you'd find it lacking.

Now that I've got mine set up where it can pick up stations and I've got the volume and tone set the way I want, all I do with the controls is switch between the same two stations on occasion. These radios are especially useful if your home office is partially or completely below ground, like in a finished basement.  Or, if you work in a metal framed office building and you want to listen to talk radio.

AM signals are directional.  You need to find the location of the transmitting tower for the station you want to listen to, and then point the radio toward the tower.  That's what I did and I can listen to radio in a place where nobody else can.

It's also a good general purpose portable radio for sitting out on your deck listening to the game or music or whatever.  It's not as bulky as a "boom box" but it's got better speakers than most portable radios, so it just sounds better in return for a slightly higher price.

Postscript:  In all fairness to those who comment on the build quality, I will say that my radio stays in one place tuned to one channel and maybe tuned to a second channel on occasion.  I hardly adjust the controls at all.  So, maybe those who are complaining about the construction quality have a point.  I'm just not using this radio in a way that involves moving it or manipulating the controls much.  It has a very easy life.

Overall, I love ASUS. The products I've bought from them and read the reviews on has made their name basically synonymous with quality products for low prices. Upon getting this monitor, I was rather impressed... a high-contrast, large, 144 Hz monitor for this cheap? Unfortunately, as a student, I don't have the extra funds to get anything more impressive than this, and my experience with ASUS told me that it would be worth the price. Overall, it absolutely is.

The software isn't too clunky, frames are consistent, contrast is utterly fantastic for the price (although you should find the optimal settings from another website, such as this one (...)), blacks and brightness are well done, there doesn't seem to be any bleeding, and the colours are (once calibrated correctly) exceptional for a monitor like this.

Unfortunately, a single pixel came stuck on arrival. This wouldn't be a HUGE issue if it were a dead pixel, as it's not shining in your face all the time, but it's always glowing red against basically any dark backdrop. I have tried things that have worked for me in the past (UnDead Pixel (UDPixel), works by cycling a 1x1 or 5x5 area of your screen through various colours very quickly in an attempt to unstick it... this has worked occasionally for several minutes, but inherently ends up failing. I've also tried pressing lightly against the spot with a soft but firm surface, like a pencil eraser (hasn't worked either)), but they fail as well.

Overall, I absolutely love this monitor. If the pixel becomes permanently unstuck I'll bump it up to a four star rating, but so many monitors getting to customers with stuck pixels is uncharacteristically bad for ASUS. If you're one of the (majority of) people who gets a monitor with NO bad pixels, I would say that it's a 5/5 monitor that you shouldn't pass up. However, if stuck pixels bother you to that extent, you may find this monitor to be a bit of a risk.

As I said, this is a fantastic monitor (aside from the stuck pixel issues people seem to have), and I want to wholeheartedly recommend it... but I can't due to this issue.
summary: Nearly perfect, but just like every other critical review, I have a stuck pixel.

reviewText: Five Stars

Perfect for younger children or those that want a simple tablet and don't need all the bells and whistles of an iPad or even a Kindle, the Genesis Prime is a solid, entry-level device.  The Genesis runs on the Android Jelly Bean 4.1 OS, comes with a 1.1 GHz processr, 512 MB of RAM and 4GB flash memory.  A micro SD slot allows you to add up to 32GB of additional space.  The HD player supports 1080P and of course is WFi capable.  It also features 5GB of Cloud storage.  The box includes a USB cable, wall charger, earphones, quick start guide, and manual.

The display of the Genesis Prime is surprisingly clear and sharp.  The tablet comes loaded with Google Play which gives you access to thousands of Android apps as well as movies, TV shows, e-books and magazines, and music.  If you don't already have one the initial setup will require you to set-up a Gmail mail account.  Initial setup was fast and easy although the first couple of times I tried to access Google Play I lost my connection to my Wi-Fi but after that initial hiccup I have not had a connection or signal issue since in the month I have been using it.  It features apps to play your music, movies, and books, along with a calendar and contact manager.

While you can stick with the Google Chrome browser that comes loaded, the processor isn't quite robust enough and Chrome can be slow and lag a bit.  I would strongly suggest downloading the Opera Mini browser which condenses web pages before loading resulting in faster browsing.  Ive used YouTube and several game apps without issue.  The speaker is on the weak and tinny side to be sure but sounds just fine with headphones or a speaker like the Braven hooked up to it.

The tablets camera can take either still pictures or video BUT, and this is a big one, is only front facing which badly limits its usefulness.  Thus if you want to take a picture of something other than yourself you cant see what you are shooting.  I don't understand if you are going to make a tablet with a camera facing only one way why you would not want to have it back facing.  Just makes no sense to me.  The tablet with last about 4 hours on a single charge which is mehok but certainly could be a lot better.

Ive read some poor reviews of the Genesis Prime but those reviews seem to forget the KEY point that the tablet is a mere $70.  The fact is you are going to be able to do a lot of the same things with this that you can with any of the yop of the line tablets for a fraction of the cost.

Sketchy, Slow, read further to know why.

On first boot, noticed it was slow, but.. knowing that typically the first boot has many processes going on in the background, after a Sysprep image is launching.

First realization there was an issue, could not connect to wifi, on any band, and with multiple access points/ routers.  Troubleshooting: connected to LAN fine, tried statically assigning IP/ DNS for WLAN, helped to connect but disconnected quickly.  Then proceeded to www.support.dell.com where I learned that Dell doesn't support windows 10 for this model of laptop.  i.e. if you have any hardware related issues, and need to download drivers / firmware, you are SOL.  See screenshot from Dell's support site, where it shows Windows 7,8,XP, etc, but not Windows 10.

2nd Issue, windows wouldn't auto activate.  License key on bottom worked, but that is not something that a "re-certified" pc would have happen.  To be classified as re-certified, the pc needs to act just as it would shipped straight from the manufacturer.  This is most likely an issue with the SYSPREP process, the seller uses.

3rd Issue, SLOOOOOOOOOWWWWWWW.  Ok, here is the tough part for the seller.  The laptop works, and looks decent, but most reviews note how slow the laptop is.  Here is why.  The hard drive passes basic testing (SMART testing/ Western Digital quick tests), but fails extensive tests, and it is obviously a drive that has bad clusters and or read write head mechanical issues.

These laptops ship with a platter based / "spinning" hard drive.  Laptops are notorious for hard drive issues, as they are moved around with much more frequency than a desktop.  Spinning platters spin between 4.2k and 7.2k rpm's, so anytime you move your laptop while it is reading/writing data, or even when its not powered on, you risk damaging the read/write head or in this case, significantly slowing down the capability of the hard drive.

Spinning / platter based hard drives usually average between 80 and 120 Mbps read/write speeds (Think Miles per hour, 80 Miles per hour, etc), with an average of 80+ (when new).  Over time, with the issues related to the drive being installed in a laptop as noted above, those speeds gradually drop.

First test w/out a load (nothing running, just chrome open), this hard drive tested w/ an average of 20 Mbps (again, compare to Miles per hour, driving hoping to get 80MPH, and with the pedal to the floor, only getting 20MPH).  As a tech, I recommend replacing hard drives that test w/ an average lower than 40 Mbps.

2nd Test, ran under a load/ with basic operations running.  Office, quickbooks, chrome, etc.  Yeah.. this got a whopping 2.3 Mbps average read/write speed.

So, we have a laptop with a failing hard drive, not supported by Manufacturer w/ the version of windows installed, oh, and with a non manufacturer/ non oem power supply (Explains why another customer noted that their charger stopped working after a few weeks).

In summary, This computer fails to meet the most basic Re-certified / refurbished standards.  I have had luck with dell refurbished laptops before, I usually just purchase straight from dell, but was on a time crunch w/ this one.  Positive note, the seller shipped it via prime, and it did arrive fast.  However, with all the issues, simply not worth the hassle.  slapping a SSD in this one, and using the devid of the wireless card, found factory firmware updates and drivers for windows 10, which fixed the network connectivity issue.
summary: Do not recommend...Not fully refurbished/recertified.  Tested/ Benchmarked by tech w/20+ years exp.

Well they support music playback and have a mic, that's about all that is good about them. The actual performance of these headphones leaves a lot to be desired. The reason I purchased these was because of reviews claiming of good audio quality (on earphones and mic), as well as the quoted 7 hour battery life. My intended use was for work, to go seamlessly from listening to music to a Google Hangout or Skype conference call and back multiple times a day. I need high quality audio with noise cancelation, these don't deliver that in any way.

If you are just listening to music, it will sound decent, but noticeably worse than even cheap wired earbuds. Once you activate the mic for a phone or conference call, it's like going back to a 90's era cell phone. The product description claims Bluetooth aptX support, but connected to my Mac and using the Bluetooth developer tools I'm unable to even force aptX codec use (necessary for good quality wireless audio over bluetooth). Paired to my iPhone, listening to music and going onto a call exhibits the same audio quality issues.

Oh, that microphone on these headphones doesn't exhibit any noise-canceling properties at all. In the office I expect it to only pickup my voice, maybe some overly loud background noises, but what I found out in testing was that even faint background noises were being picked up and transmitted to the receiving party. Outdoors on a quiet neighborhood street I had to shout to be heard above what was at most a 5mph wind.

In both sound quality departments, these are far inferior to the Apple EarPods bundled with every iPhone going back a few years. Guess I'll have to try a different product.
summary: Look elsewhere if you want quality

I bought the Sennheiser HD555 from Amazon this week, exclusively for use with my IPod Touch. I already own the UE Super.fi 5 Pro canal phones and they are great indeed, but I was wanting a set of headphones for both work and home that were easier to put on and take off.  The Super.fi Pros take a few moments to get the seal right.  I must say that I was rather disappointed with the HD555.  So much so, that on the following day  I  purchased the Bose On-Ear headphones. Yes, the Sennheiser HD555 have a more defined midrange and more pronounced high's than the Bose On-Ears do.  But why is it that I was so unsatisfied when listening to them?  I listened to the Bose headphones, and enjoyed their presentation far more than the HD555's.  I played a orchestra/vocal mp3, "Gollum's Song", with Emiliana Torrini, and recorded at 320 sampling rate rate, and the HD555 sounded better than the Bose, so I will add my confirmation to the others, that for classical and orchestrated music the HD555 will noticeably outperform the Bose On-Ear's.  ...But.  The Bose did quite well with that and other orchestra pieces too and just gave such a more well-rounded performance on all different types of music than the HD555 did. Amongst many other songs, I listened to the Beatles' "Come Together" and the HD555's disappointed badly there, and I had to turn the EQ bass booster on to get any satisfaction at all from it. The batteries are SigmasTek that I just received.  I am not sure how the brand will stack up, but they are about half the cost of a genuine RBC7.  Keep in mind this listing/product has had various sellers over the years.  The current seller is BatterySharks.com and you can buy these $3 cheaper on their site (not sure if it ships as fast though, I have Prime).

It's a simple process to setup the batteries...place them so the connectors are in the middle (one positive will be next to the other's negative).  Pop the terminal covers off your original battery (held on by 4 pieces of double-sided foam tape).  If you have double-sided foam tape that can be used to tie the batteries together, but you have be accurate...and easier method is to hook up the fusible link and then simply run a piece of packing tap across to top width-wise and then a couple pieces around the sides and bottom....make a 3" tape flap at the fuse end so you can pull the battery out next time.  Connect the power leads (make sure positive and negative are correct)...pop the two terminal covers back on and as you have it about ready to slide in connect the plug inside the UPS to the new battery....pop it in and you are back in business after a couple screws and putting the cover back on.

With Smart UPS 1500's and IBM 2130R5X/UPS1500TLV's these can be done without turning off the UPS and without having to power down any connected devices (hot-swapable).

Even with my genuine RBC7, I am lucky to get 2 years out of a battery set as I am coastal and the power flucuates constantly turning the day.  If I get more than a year out of these, I am still ahead.  They come in a sealed factory box as well, some vendors ship used batteries that are almost impossible to tell from new (other than getting much less life) or batteries that have been sitting on a shelf for a year+ which also will have shorter lives.
summary: Great deal, currently shipping SigmasTek batteries.

I agree with the reviews that speak of the good features of this tripod... it is lightweight, easy to set up, compacts to a reasonable size, and is not difficult to carry.

I purchased this tripod in 2004 but have never used it with my video camera; it always held my still camera. This year, I began using my video camera and a tripod was needed for smooth panning and tilt for an hour-long shoot. The subject was a corporate trainer whose motions did not follow a predictable path.

The first taping, I found the joints a little sticky, even though the clamps were loosened. To prepare for the next taping, I attempted to lubricate he mechanism. That is when I realized that the design and construction was the cause and not that the tripod needed the lubricant.

The construction of the joints had large clearances thus the tradeoff was keeping the adjustment snug or allowing the maximum freedom to eliminate the stickiness. On the second taping, I loosened everything up and was more careful. Some erratic movement could be edited out and some was compensated by the video camera's steady-cam features.

While I like this tripod for my still pictures I would suggest evaluating other tripods for video use when panning, or tilt is needed.

Having finally made the move to a 3.0 Hub I am extra pleased.  As far as USB Hubs go, this one has pleased me in a number of ways.

Size - From time to time I've been given some free "swag" USB hubs by vendors wanting to promote their company.  Some of these were insanely large for the number of ports and capability they provided.  This Sabrent 7-Port Hub is similar in size to a pack of playing cards.  It takes up very little desktop space but is still large enough to have something plugged into all 7 ports without trouble.

Speed - Naturally, the main benefit I saw immediately on upgrade was speed.  Going from USB 2 to USB 3 is fabulous.  My hard drives can now transfer at full capabilities.  My phone charges much faster.  It's lovely.

Power Switch - When I first got this, I wasn't sure why I would necessarily care about having a separate power switch for each port on the hub.  Then I remembered experiences I'd had with an older hub where having multiple high power USB devices plugged in at a time would result in some of them not being recognized (due to not being served enough power to run).  In the past, I would have to unplug on or more devices to get another one to run and then I'd have to find the plug and plug it back in later.  Being able to leave the cable plugged in and just press a button is handy.  It's still not a feature I use a lot but it's kind of cool.

I use an iPad Pro for work with clients off-site, and a keyboard (and machine protection) is a must-have. This combination case is as good as we've found, but the detractions were far too great for me.

First, the positives. The case weighs about as much as the iPad, so together you're looking at about two pounds. For some that detracts from the levity of the machine, but the alternative, for me, is a light laptop--so I'd be looking at two-pounds either way, and likely more. When the case is closed, the iPad is totally protected, enclosed inside the hard plastic that's as tasteful as plastic gets. I felt confident enough just slipping the whole unit into my briefcase until in-field work time. Also, the magnetic catch system works well to hold the iPad up for viewing or typing.

But the most important aspect of a keyboard, to me, is the typing experience. And after trying four other portable bluetooth keyboards, I'm not impressed with what I've found so far because important keys are often moved about to save space. On this Belkin keyboard, for example, the return/enter key, the right shift key, the (right) semicolon/colon key, the apstrophe/quotes key, and the right quote key are all at unexpected places or too near/too far for me to easily get accustomed to.

If this were the only keyboard I used, I supposed I'd become acclimated to it, but switching back and forth between this and standard keyboards just won't work. I never get used to the layout of the Belkin keyboard. It's extremely frustrating to have to lift my hands off the keyboard to check where the above-mentioned right keys sit, or if I think I've finally gotten the feel of the keyboard and type without looking, to find myself returning-new-line instead of inserting an apostrophe or shifting...

The feel of the case and keyboard is about as good as I've found, and the protection for the iPad is outstanding. But I couldn't get used to the Belkin's layout. To contrast, I bought the original iPad six to seven years ago and paired it with a Logitec bluetooth keyboard. That keyboard's layout so effectively mimics a standard keyboard's that today, years after my original iPad has ceased working, I still use the Logitec keyboard, pairing it with my phone or my Lenovo tablet or even my laptop when I take it into the field for presentations, so I can type while a group is viewing my files.

At least I've concluded that any keyboard that changes the orientation of the main keys--including shift, return, apostrophe/quotes, colon/semicolon, cannot compensate with other desirables. One final note:  if possible, especially with these high-tactile devices, try to borrow one from a friend for a week or so to see if it will work for you. You should know in a few days. If I'd bought this from a local Best Buy, I'd have returned it within 48 hours.
summary: Terrific iPad protector, but poor right-keys orientation may create significant typing liability

In short, I'm glad I waited.

Our Harmony 880 finally started to die on us after years of service. Not sure what it was that was killing the IR, but it finally wouldn't control our devices. We had been putting off the upgrade because:

At first, the Harmony One was getting long in the tooth. We knew there were newer ones coming, so we waited.

The Harmony Link seemed cool! Then we heard that it required an always-on internet connection to work and the settings were all stored online. If the server went down, a connection was temporarily lost, or your internet so much as looked at you sideways, it would stop working. This was unacceptable, so we waited.

The Harmony Touch seemed to be a bad layout with no other benefit over the Harmony One, so we waited.

All the while, only one device could be associated with one account. That's nearly inexcusable. A different email address for each device is required? Who thought that was a good idea?

The Harmony Ultimate solves all of these problems except for one, which I will get to in a moment. Your configuration is stored locally on the Hub, so if your internet connection goes down, it is no longer an issue! Fantastic! When you use the app (which is phone only, not tablet. I hope this is fixed in the near future) it pulls the configuration and information from the hub, and the hub keeps all devices in sync as opposed to a server online. Moreover, all devices remain aware of the current state of the home entertainment system and devices. If I turn on Watch TV with the remote, the phone says Watch TV is active and so on. Fixed the Link's problem!

The Ultimate is the newest model, with what appears to be a super-reliable charging cradle. So while the One is good it shows its age in comparison to the Ultimate. I just set the hub where it can see my whole entertainment center and it no longer matters where I'm sitting. No more doing the volume dance where I try to find a line of sight to the stereo with the remote that's in my hand. I just hit volume, and the hub sends it no matter where I am. Fixed the One's problem!

Also, your account now allows multiple devices! Fixed that too!

Here's the one thing they didn't fix. Vs the Touch, the screen still sits below the play/pause. When I have to hit those buttons, I have to carefully avoid hitting the touch screen, which is now a gesture control which could accidentally fast-forward or such. This was a horrible decision they haven't yet fixed. That said, it's no dealbreaker as I can still use the remote; it's just more difficult. This is the sole reason I give it 4 stars instead of 5.

Other than that, the remote is surprisingly small. Smaller than the 880, so my thumb can actually reach the whole thing if needs be. The tilt sensor is vastly improved as well, so when I pick it up, I don't need to shake it to make it wake. Very nice.

My only suggestions for future improvements are as follows:

Move the play/pause/FF/Rew below the touchscreen. For the love of all things good, do this in the next iteration.

And two, now that a website is synced with the hub... let me control the entertainment center using the app remotely. I don't mean from somewhere in the house. I mean when I'm not in the state. I know it's a weird thing to ask for, but when we're visiting family, it would be nice to turn on Animal Planet for the dog to keep her from barking all the time, or set a schedule that turns the TV on like an alarm clock, but only on weekdays or such. Also, it would be great if we could turn the whole system off when we realize we're going to be gone longer than we thought that night. We could also turn the TV on as a "We're home, don't break in!" measure remotely. These are all nice-to-have compared to moving the screen though.

Lastly, please provide a tablet version of your app for both iOS and Android! Maybe a Window 8/RT/Phone app? And please, please, please put it on Amazon's App Store. There's no reason not to, and there are probably millions of Kindle Fires out there that could be remotes for this awesome hub!

I can not say enough good things about this remote though. It is the first suitable replacement for the One or the 880 that i have seen to date. Very well done. If you have fewer devices, the less expensive $129 will only have 3 activities on the remote, and I don't know if it limits the app, but it also has the hub. (which is awesome)

I have been running two D-Link DCS-1100 wired IP cams for over three months now.

PROS: This is a reasonably priced, solid camera with a fairly broad range of functions. I have successfully used the FTP feature to upload images every few seconds to an archive server on the both the LAN and WAN sides of my cameras. In general the camera tends to keep working and not freeze up. The streaming video image is best viewed from the home page of the web based control interface.

CONS: My biggest problem with the DCS-1100 is that the web based control interface cannot be used at all in Firefox and tends to freeze up in Safari. If you're like me and you don't use Internet Explorer for security reasons (especially all those Active-X goodies), you're likely to have difficulties configuring and managing this camera. Also the ability to insert streaming videos into a web page doesn't seem to work reliably or consistently for anything other than IE, and even then there are some issues. Finally the light range is adequate at best which means that in order to get any night vision at all, I am obliged to suffer a bit too much brightness during the day.

One of my two IPCAMS replaced a USB webcam, but since I didn't have the option of continuing to run a USB webcam, my best guess is that, notwithstanding its faults, there is nothing better than the DCS-1100 for anything near to its price range.

After connecting everything, a simple double hit of the "Scroll Lock" key seamlessly transfers control between the two machines.  After reading some negatives on sound quality, I decided to do a test and compare the sound on my new PC between using the switch and directly connecting the speakers to the desktop.  My speakers are nothing to write home about, but I could not tell any substantial difference between the direct connection and going through the switch.  You mileage may vary depending on your speakers.  One item to note is that the switch only workers with externally powered speakers.  The speakers on my old PC plugged in through a special port that powered them so they did not work.  Luckily I already had another set that had its own power source.  The one thing the switch will not do is connect the microphone on my monitor.  I really don't use it so this is not a problem for me.  When choosing a KVM switch, you should make sure that all of the components that you want to share have a connection on the switch.  Overall, this is a very solid product for the limited scope that I needed.

I purchased two of the AJ130 alarm clock/CD/radios on December 4, 2007,
from another online retailer, and was excited to do so, as my wife and I are owners of other Philips clock radios with the "Gentle Wake" feature (She has the AJ3965 and I have the AJ3980).  My intent was to buy two matching, smaller, sleek models with similar functions to the ones we were replacing.  Both of us really like the "Gentle Wake" feature of the Philips line.  I set both of the clocks up, and, to my dismay, the Gentle Wake feature, which is advertised as included on this model, does not function.  I figured that, perhaps, one was defective and that I might have to return it, but then when the feature didn't work on EITHER of them, I thought better and wrote to Philips, asking them whether or not he Gentle Wake feature, said to be one of this model's features, actually exists in this model.  A phone call solved nothing -- upon my suggestion that they consider bench/lab testing this model for that function, the tech support guy told me that they weren't able to do that.  How about that?!?!  The MANUFACTURER of the darn clock can't even test it.  Makes you wonder.

Really, my only complaint about the unit is the fact that BOTH new units lack the touted "Gentle Wake" feature.  It is not a misprint or an error on the website -- it is advertised on the unit's packaging.  I'm also very familiar with how the feature works.  On the other two models I mentioned, the Gentle Wake gradually increases the volume of whatever the wake-up setting is (radio/CD/buzzer) until it reaches a maximum level.  In fact, on the AJ3965, you can even set what the maximum level you want it to reach IS.  On the AJ130, the Gentle Wake is only applicable to the BUZZER setting, so CD and Radio do not gradually get louder -- they stay at whatever level you have the volume set at before you go to sleep.  When the alarm goes off, though, if you have it set on "Buzzer," the volume goes straight for the jugular -- there ain't NOTHIN' "Gentle" about that "Wake."

It's a sad situation, because Philips makes good products, but I think they really goofed with this one.  It might turn out that they just happened to manufacture a "bad batch" of them, but I have a feeling that this is more than just a bad batch.  I question whether or not the Gentle Wake feature REALLY IS supposed to be promoted as included on this model.

I've written to Philips Consumer Electronics about this problem.  I'm somewhat leery of sending them my clocks for an exchange, as I'm afraid that the two that I receive in return will lack the same functionality, and what's more -- I'll be out whatever it cost me to ship them.

I don't know.  Buy at your own risk.  I only say that I would NOT recommend it to a friend because of the fact that the feature is absent when it is supposed to be present.  If they fix that issue, then I would recommend it.

I only have 2 gripes:

2. I really wish the dock came in black, considering that the drives are black. The white makes it look like an Apple product.

Also note that there are 2 variants of this product.
1. The FreeAgent Go Dock+ has 3 powered USB ports, effectively making this a USB hub for only a few dollars more.
2. The FreeAgent Go DockStar also has 3 powered USB ports as well as a network/Ethernet port which effectively turns this into a NAS that can be accessed from any computer on the same network. This model, however, is substantially more expensive.

In general, it does what it does pretty well, but there is a lot it doesn't do (and doesn't even try to do).  As long as you know what to expect, it is a decent unit, but certainly not a perfect media player.

For example, just straight-up playing videos over the LAN is fantastic.  Quality of video and sound is excellent (assuming the video source is also good)
However, trying to navigate through the video to points is frustrating or just bizarre....for example:
- Chapters don't work.  If you try to use the next/previous chapter buttons on your control you'll end up jumping to the next/previous media FILE not CHAPTER.  Needless to say this is maddening.
- You can skip to a percentage of the video by pressing the 1-9 buttons, which will jump you to that 10% of the file.  e.g. pressing 7 will take you to 70% of the way through the movie.
- FFW/RWD only go at double speed.  Nothing more, nothing less, and when you press play again you often end up playing up to 10 seconds away from the point you pressed the button at.
- PageUp/PageDn.  Yup, when watching a video they jump you forward 30 seconds or backwards 15 seconds.  Useful but peculiar.

Audio is again good but the unit's slow interface can make this a bit of a chore.  The sounds quality is fantastic (depending on your speakers of course, and also assuming a good quality of the ripped file)
However, once again the system makes you jump through hoops or struggle to figure out how best to use it....for example:
- Browsing to a ripped CD through the Album option gives the album tracks in a different order than when you browse to the album through the Artist option.  One is in alphabetical order, the other is in the correct album order.  Why on earth would you want album tracks in alphabetical order???
- There doesn't appear to be a way to just play randomly/shuffle across your entire collection (or even a subset of it).  Surely this wouldn't be hard to implement?  I find this strangely lacking.

Other observations:
1) While waiting for my new HDMI cable I initially ran this over Component.  Don't do it!  The ratio on many of my video files was wrong and vertically stretched.  Relatively speaking this was only out by an inch or so, but the result was that everything looked weird.  As soon as I sent the output over HDMI it went back to normal.
2) I use a master-switching power strip for most of my electronics.  If you're unfamiliar with them, when one specific device is turned off, it powers off the other sockets on the strip to save energy.  However when I ran the 520 on one of those switched sockets, it would routinely reset itself to factory defaults!  I have no idea why this was happening, perhaps it was something with the way the power trigger interacted with the power on signal to the device from the remote, but I was minutes away from sending it back before I decided to try it on a 'real' power socket.  I haven't had any issues since I did that, and it was resetting about once per day before.
3) It does play some video formates not listed, but only to an extent.  For example, I was VERY pleased to see it play VOB files which is a common format for just ripping DVDs.  The only problem is that a DVD ripped to VOBs is actually stored in a number of 1GB VOB files.  When it reaches the end of one VOB file, it stops and doesn't move on the the next file in the movie.  Its not a big deal for me since I know this wasn't even supposed to be supported, but its sooooo close to working right that its just a little frustrating.
4) There are a number of video or audio formats I would like to have seen (e.g. DivX, even ISO perhaps).  I knew these weren't supported so they don't affect my score as such, I just mention it as part of my reasoning for why its 'not a perfect media player'.

Overall, I like the unit, and I got it at an excellent price.  I would not have paid more for it, but I would recommend it if someone can get it for about a hundred after rebates.  I anticipate that this will be a short term thing for me (a year or two), before I get a newer generation one that has as more rounded set of features.  Just be aware of the limitations and you'll be fine.

Hopefully future firmware updates might fix some things, like the shuffle to the music or the album track listing order problem, but its been a while since a new one has been released so I get the feeling DLink are moving on to newer models and leaving this behind.

Sony makes a very reliable blank CD-R that can handle up to 80 minutes of music or 700 megabytes of data. Moreover, these blank CD-Rs are capable of recording data at high speeds. (I looked at one older Sony CD-R disc to help me write this review--would you believe it DIDN'T say the speed at which it records? Sorry!!!) The data I record onto these CD-Rs has now lasted for over three years, proving the test of time. I have used these as data discs and discs to record audio. I almost never got a coaster. Great!

The CD-R discs are compact and easy to store. While the discs are still blank, store them in the circular case on the spindle that they came in. After your burn data or music onto them, I would recommend storing them in slim jewel cases instead of paper sleeves. It's just better protection for your CD-Rs that have anything stored on them. Don't store these discs, burnt or blank, in rooms that become very hot; this causes damage to any brand of this type of disc and you could lose data over time.

There are two caveats that many other people note about any brand of this product: when you are burning the data onto the blank disc, don't be surprised if you see that the data is burning at a rate slower than the packaging advertises. This can happen if your burner doesn't have the capacity to burn faster, or it may be a quirk. I am not a professional so I cannot be certain of precisely what causes this phenomenon; but I assure you that the extra minute or two (tops) that you wait to get your CD-R completed is worth the wait. In addition, DON'T write on these using Sharpie ink pens. The ink can seep through the top coating of the CD-R disc and slowly but surely compromise your data--and you wouldn't want that, now would you? If you need to label the discs, label its' jewel case using a post-it note. At least that's what I do.

Overall, Sony blank CD-R discs store data reliably over the years and I believe that an extra minute to burn the data onto the blank disc is well worth it in the event that it doesn't actually burn at the very highest speed advertised.

Use them in good health!

reviewText:
I wanted a new case for my Asrock Z87E-ITX motherboard because the old one was a bit large for the vintage buffet that I'm using for an entertainment console. I also wanted a case that would let me install a slot-loading Blu-ray drive. There aren't a lot of choices out there, so I was really happy to find the ML-06.

Construction is solid, as you would expect, and there were no surprises when it came to opening up the case.  I was pleased to see that Silverstone hadn't used any oddball fasteners; they were all Philips-head screws. However, I thought it was odd that they used silver screws to attach the top panel and the power supply given that the case is black.

I had Silverstone's SFX power supply in the old case, so I just moved it over along with the motherboard. Power supply goes in first, and you WILL need the modular cables for it, because space is at a heavy premium when you get everything installed. The motherboard drops in and attaches with 4 screws. I moved the pair of 2.5" hard drives from the old case into the drive cage (I also have an mSATA drive attached directly to the motherboard). Although Silverstone says you can put 4 drives in the cage, poor placement of one set of holes (at least in my unit) means you can really only put in 3. And given the lack of room in the case, you can really only put 2 drives in the case because you need the space in the cage to stuff some of the wires.

I attached my Blu-ray drive to the bottom of the multipurpose bracket, and then went to put it back in the case. I was disappointed to find out that my Zalman CPU cooler, which I though was pretty low-profile, is too tall; the bracket will go back in on its own, but not with the drive hanging from it. Dang! I guess at some point I can get a new CPU cooler, but for now, I'll go back to using the Blu-ray from an external box.

The case has space on the right side for a pair of 80mm fans, but I didn't bother. The PSU and CPU fans provide enough exhaust, though if I do install the Blu-ray drive, it will block the CPU fan's access to the top vent, and then I might need at least one of those side fans.

The front audio and USB 3 ports are on the right side of the case, which is a bit nonstandard. If the space you're putting the case in is a little tight, this might be a consideration for you. For me, it's not an issue.

After I reattached all the cables, I put the top back on, attached the power cord, the USB WiFi, the USB transmitter for the wireless keyboard, and the HDMI cable, and it was off the races! Everything is working fine, and the ML-06 fits great in the available space in the console. I'm a happy camper!

You may read in some reviews that some levels of motor noise should be present in modern mini-DV cameras, due to its compact size (mic too close to motor). In my experience that is not true, as my new Panasonic does not present any noise.

If you are looking for a camera to use for images only (editing the sound or including soundtrack), the Canon Elura 100 is still a great option due to its superior picture quality (larger sensor 1/5"), but if sound is important to you, think twice before buying it.

A couple of notes about "signal strength." Signal strength is measured in decibels (dB), a logarithmic scale (each 3 dB of loss reduces the signal power by about half). Connectors typically introduce ~ 0.01dB, or less than 1% power loss. Even poor quality connectors usually keep loss under 0.1dB (about 2% power loss). Comparatively, a 100 foot RG6 cable loses ~ 4dB (it varies between the high and low ends of the broadcast spectrum range). So compared to the loss in your cable run, a connector is likely to be a negligent factor in signal quality. It is of course possible for a connector to push the signal over its tipping point, but this would be the exception rather than the rule. It is also possible to get a bad apple that slipped passed QA. There are other manufacturers of this component as well, such as Cable Matters and Mediabridge. Quality connectors are also available from Mouser.

reviewText: Good thing it was a gift...

This is a cute, inexpensive bluetooth speak that works great.  It's not going to put out the volume or bass of a much bigger, much more expensive speaker but on the other hand this one will fit in a pocket in your backpack and really improve the sound from your phone.

As a bonus it works as a speakerphone, it has a built-in microphone that will let you use your phone as a hands free phone in the car or while sitting at your desk.  It paired up easily with my Mac and with a Nexus phone.

It has an aux audio input jack, a micro USB port for charging and four simple buttons on top (Power, Pause/Play, Back and Forward).  Two of the buttons also serve as volume up/down buttons.  I'm not real fond of the volume buttons, you have to press and hold to use them as volume buttons, if you press and release they'll act as forward/back buttons which will likely result in you either restarting a song or skipping to the next one when you don't want.

I haven't had it long enough to determine how long it will last on a charge.  There is a dual use LED that is blue when connected over Bluetooth and alternates with a red flash when charging.

I received this New Trent product at a reduced price in return for a fair and reliable review based on my user experience.

Update:
After making sure the speaker was fully charged I ran it for 8 hours last night playing white noise at low volume, this is not an accurate test of longevity for music played louder but I did want to see if it lasted all night.  White noise helps some people sleep better.  The result was it was still playing after 8 hours.

Update 2:
I was able to get 8+ hrs of music at a moderate volume.  However, when used to watch a movie there was a lag between that audio and video that was noticeable to the point of being annoying.  I repeated the test with a Bose Soundlink and the lag was nearly imperceptible.  Of course the Bose was > 10x as much.  In addition the audio would cut in and out when used to watch a movie on an Apple computer, I didn't experience the same dropouts on the Bose.  It may be that the speaker is designed to reduce power when no audio is playing but if that is the case it isn't doing a good job.  Normal music is fine, no dropouts.  I took off a star for the dropouts, not really planning on watching movies with it so not important to me.

Lastly, I opened the case to examine the components.  A standard LiOn battery is used, if you have soldering skills you can replace the battery.  The speaker is a 4 ohm, 5W speaker.
summary: Small, compact, good sound, reasonable price
